About this simulation

On screen
Left: the current I (mA) and the potential difference V across the component (V) against t from 0 to 600 ms, with the previous run in faint grey, a thin line at every throw of the switch, and after each throw a dotted tangent running to the value the trace is heading for, with a tick at the meeting point. Right: the schematic with the switch S, the reference arrow I, a moving arrow whose length follows |I| and points the way the current flows, and +/− signs on the capacitor plates.
Controls
Component chooses the capacitor or the ideal inductor. Switch S (its buttons, the switch in the schematic, the Throw button or the S key) moves the switch; the first throw to position 1 starts the clock. R, C and L set the circuit; changing any of them, or ⟲ New run, ends the run, keeps its traces in grey, discharges the component and returns S to position 2.
Measured
t in ms from the first throw, I in mA along the reference arrow and V in volts (the potential where the arrow enters the component less that of the other terminal), from the exact RC and RL transients; the clock runs 20 times slower than real time. On the closing card and in free exploration the Readouts panel adds the time constant (RC or L/R) and the energy stored in the component, ½CV2 or ½LI2.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Charging the capacitor

Put the capacitor in the slot with R = 100 Ω and C = 400 μF; the capacitor starts uncharged, with the switch in position 2. Before throwing the switch to position 1, predict the current I and the potential difference V across the capacitor just after the throw. Then throw it and watch both graphs.

2 · Switching the capacitor back

Keep the settings of question 1 and let the run go on until the current has fallen close to zero and V is nearly 6.0 V. Before moving the switch to position 2, predict what the current does just after the move.

3 · Switching on the inductor

Put the inductor in the slot with R = 100 Ω and L = 4 H, which gives the same time constant of 40 ms, and leave the switch in position 2. Before throwing the switch to position 1, predict the current I and the potential difference V across the inductor just after the throw. Then throw it and compare the traces with the grey ones left by the capacitor.

4 · Switching the inductor back

Keep the settings of question 3 and let the run go on until the current has settled close to 60 mA. Before moving the switch to position 2, predict what the current through the inductor does just after the move.

5 · The inductor with more resistance

Keep the inductor with L = 4 H and change R to 200 Ω, which ends the run and leaves its traces in grey. Before throwing the switch to position 1, predict how the growth of the current compares with the grey trace.

6 · The capacitor with more resistance

Keep R at 200 Ω, put the capacitor back in the slot and set C = 400 μF. Before throwing the switch to position 1, predict how the capacitor's current compares with its run at 100 Ω in question 1, which started at 60 mA with a time constant of 40 ms.

7 · What to take away

Across a capacitor the potential difference V = Q/C cannot jump, so at a throw it is the current that jumps. Through an inductor the current cannot jump, so it is V = L dI/dt that jumps.

Every transient approaches its final value exponentially, with τ = RC for the capacitor and τ = L/R for the inductor; the dotted tangent at each throw meets the final value one τ later.

A larger R slows the capacitor, since τ = RC grows, but speeds up the inductor, since τ = L/R shrinks. The Readouts panel now also shows τ and the energy stored.

The Physics

Switching a Capacitor and an Inductor · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

This sim puts a resistor R in series with a capacitor or an ideal inductor. A two-way switch S joins them to a 6.0 V source in position 1 and closes the loop on itself in position 2. Two graphs follow the current I and the potential difference V after each throw of S.

What you'll learn

  • What I and V do at the instant S is thrown, and in the time after it.
  • What sets the pace, and how R, C and L change it.
  • Where the energy of the source goes.
The circuit in the sim, sketched: the source ℰ, the switch S with contacts 1 and 2, the resistor R and the slot for C or L. The arrow is the direction taken as positive for the current I.

What's on screen

  • The top graph is the current I in mA against t, from 0 to 600 ms. A bar along the top fills as the clock runs.
  • The lower graph is the potential difference V in volts. Each throw of S adds a thin line, labelled 1 or 2, and a dotted tangent drawn to the value the trace is heading for.
  • Grey traces are the previous run, kept for comparison until you start another.
  • The circuit and the readouts: Time t, Current I, P.d. V, Time constant τ and Energy stored.
See itLook at the opening state, before S is thrown. Watch for: Time t reading 0.0 ms, Current I reading 0.0 mA, and P.d. V reading 0.0 V, with S in position 2.

03

A capacitor holds its potential difference, so at the throw the current jumps to ℰ/R

An uncharged capacitor has V = Q/C = 0, and Q cannot change in an instant, because charge arrives only as current. When S is thrown to 1, all of ℰ falls across R. The loop law, with I = dQ/dt, is (notes 4.32)

At t = 0 it gives I = ℰ/R = 60.0 mA for R = 100 Ω. As charge piles up, V rises, less of ℰ is left across R, and the current dies away (notes 4.33):

With R = 100 Ω and C = 400 μF, τ = 40 ms.
The capacitor after the throw to 1 at t = 0. I jumps to 60 mA and dies away. V climbs from 0 towards ℰ. The dotted tangents reach the final values at t = τ.

At t = τ = 40 ms, I = 22.1 mA and V = 3.79 V. At 200 ms, I = 0.40 mA and V = 5.96 V.

Key idea. A capacitor's potential difference cannot jump, so its current can. With the capacitor empty, the circuit behaves as if it were a plain wire.
See itThrow S to 1 with the capacitor in the slot, and look at the first instant. Watch for: Time t reading 0.0 ms, Current I reading 60.0 mA, and P.d. V reading 0.0 V.
04

An inductor holds its current, so at the throw the potential difference jumps to ℰ

A coil opposes any change of current through it. Across an ideal inductor, V = L dI/dt (notes 4.28), so a jump in I would need an infinite V. With I = 0 at the throw nothing falls across R, and all of ℰ falls across L (notes 4.39):

At t = 0, V = ℰ = 6.0 V and I starts to rise at ℰ/L = 1.5 A/s, which is 1.5 mA per ms for L = 4 H. As I grows, more of ℰ falls across R, so V falls (notes 4.40):

With R = 100 Ω and L = 4 H, τ = 40 ms.
The inductor after the throw to 1 at t = 0. V jumps to ℰ and dies away. I rises from 0 towards ℰ/R. The dotted tangents reach the final values at t = τ.

At t = τ = 40 ms, I = 37.9 mA and V = 2.21 V. At 200 ms, I = 59.6 mA and V = 0.04 V.

Key idea. An inductor's current cannot jump, so its potential difference can. The two components swap roles: the capacitor's I and the inductor's V start at their largest value, and the other quantity starts at 0.
See itPut the inductor in the slot, throw S to 1, and look at the first instant. Watch for: Time t reading 0.0 ms, Current I reading 0.0 mA, and P.d. V reading 6.0 V.
05

Thrown back to 2, the capacitor's current reverses but the inductor's keeps its direction

In position 2 the source is out of the loop, and the component discharges through R. Throw S back at t = 200 ms, when each has all but finished charging.

The capacitor still holds V = 5.96 V, so it now drives a current V/R = 59.6 mA through R against the old direction (notes 4.29–4.31):

Q0 is the charge at the throw back. The negative sign means the reverse direction.

The inductor still carries I = 59.6 mA. Its induced emf keeps that current flowing the same way (notes 4.41):

I1 is the current at the throw back, t1 = 200 ms.
The current I for both components, with S thrown to 1 at 0 and back to 2 at 200 ms. The capacitor's I reverses. The inductor's I keeps its sign.

Key idea. What a component holds across the throw is what carries on: the capacitor its V, the inductor its I. The other quantity jumps.
See itCharge the capacitor for 200 ms, then throw S back to 2. Watch for: Current I reading −59.6 mA, the reverse direction, while P.d. V stays at 6.0 V.
See itDo the same with the inductor in the slot. Watch for: Current I still reading 59.6 mA, while P.d. V reads −6.0 V.
06

Every transient closes on its final value by a factor e in each τ

All four curves obey one rule. A quantity X that starts at X0 and is heading for Xfinal follows

τ = RC for a capacitor and τ = L/R for an inductor. X is I or V.

In each time τ the gap to the final value shrinks by the factor 1/e = 0.368. The tangent at the start reaches the final value at t = τ, which is the dotted line the sim draws and labels in ms.

Key idea. After 5τ a transient is 99 % complete, so the pace of every curve is set by τ alone.
See itThrow S to 1 with the capacitor in the slot, and stop at t = τ. Watch for: Time t reading 40.0 ms, Time constant τ reading 40 ms, Current I reading 22.1 mA, and P.d. V reading 3.8 V.
See itDo the same with the inductor in the slot. Watch for: Time t reading 40.0 ms, Current I reading 37.9 mA, and P.d. V reading 2.2 V.
07

More resistance slows the capacitor but speeds up the inductor

τ = RC grows with R, and τ = L/R shrinks. A capacitor must pass the charge Cℰ through R, and a larger R means a smaller current to carry it, so the charging is slower. An inductor starts at the same slope ℰ/L = 1.5 mA per ms whatever R is, but a larger R lowers the final current ℰ/R, which is therefore reached sooner.

The current I after the throw to 1, at R = 100 Ω and 200 Ω. Top, the inductor reaches 30 mA instead of 60 mA, with τ = 20 ms instead of 40 ms. Bottom, the capacitor starts at 30 mA instead of 60 mA, with τ = 80 ms.

Key idea. The same R acts on the two components in opposite ways, because one has ℰ/R as its starting current and the other as its final current.
See itPut the inductor in the slot, set R to 200 Ω, throw S to 1, and stop at t = 20 ms. Watch for: Time constant τ reading 20 ms and Current I reading 19.0 mA, which is 63 % of 30 mA.
See itPut the capacitor in the slot at R = 200 Ω, throw S to 1, and stop at t = 80 ms. Watch for: Time constant τ reading 80 ms, Current I reading 11.0 mA, and P.d. V reading 3.8 V.
08

Charging a capacitor stores half the source's work, and the resistor turns the other half into heat

Multiply the loop law by I = dQ/dt (notes 4.37):

The left side is the power of the source, the first term on the right heats R, and the second is the rate at which the capacitor's stored energy grows.

The source moves the charge Cℰ through ℰ, so it does the work Cℰ² = 14.4 mJ. The capacitor ends with ½Cℰ² = 7.20 mJ, the value of Energy stored. The heat is (notes 4.38)

The result does not depend on R.
The energy account while the capacitor charges, for R = 100 Ω and C = 400 μF. At R = 200 Ω the figures are the same, reached more slowly.

The inductor keeps the same account. Multiplying 4.39 by I gives ℰI = I²R + d(½LI²)/dt (notes 4.42). For L = 4 H and I = 60 mA the coil stores ½LI² = 7.20 mJ, and when S is thrown back all of it is turned into heat in R.

Key idea. The work of the source beyond the heating of R is stored: ½Cℰ² in the capacitor, ½LI² in the coil. For the capacitor, the heat is exactly the other half.
See itLet the capacitor charge until t = 300 ms. Watch for: Energy stored reading 7.19 mJ, within 0.1 % of ½Cℰ² = 7.20 mJ.
See itDo the same with the inductor in the slot. Watch for: Energy stored again reading 7.19 mJ, now ½LI² at I = 59.97 mA.
09

Summary

In one line. This sim throws a switch to connect a resistor and either a capacitor or an ideal inductor to a 6.0 V source, and shows how the current and the potential difference change in the time after each throw.

Key points

  • A capacitor holds its V and an inductor holds its I. The other quantity jumps.
  • Every transient closes on its final value as e−t/τ, with τ = RC or τ = L/R.
  • Raising R slows the capacitor and speeds up the inductor. Charging a capacitor heats R with ½Cℰ², whatever R is.

Common mix-ups

  • "A capacitor blocks current, so I starts at zero." An empty capacitor passes the full ℰ/R = 60 mA at the throw. A full one passes almost none.
  • "An ideal inductor has no resistance, so the current jumps to ℰ/R." The current starts at 0 and climbs at 1.5 mA per ms. It is 37.9 mA at 40 ms.
  • "Take the source away and the inductor's current stops." It carries on in the same direction: 59.6 mA at the throw back.
  • "More resistance slows everything." It slows the capacitor, τ = 80 ms at 200 Ω, and speeds up the inductor, τ = 20 ms.

Things to try on your own

  • Set the capacitor to R = 200 Ω and C = 200 μF, and compare τ and the starting current with the opening values.
